correctness.rationale: Fresh independent C++17 exact enumerator generated class counts 1,1,2,4,12,56,456,6880 via complete vertex-extension and explicit adjacency-preserving isomorphism recursion. It constructed every nonempty face contained in a vertex out-neighborhood and oriented integer boundary matrices. Unit Smith pivots were eliminated unimodularly, and every remaining submatrix was exactly zero for all 6880 complexes, hence all boundary images are primitive and integral homology has no torsion. Fresh histogram reproduced all 26 advertised multiplicities (sum 6880). Independently checked the extremal representative via SymPy: f=(8,28,19,4), reduced ranks give (0,6,0). Six-vertex RP2 positive control has SNF(d2) with nine units and one factor 2. Proof is exhaustive finite computation only, not a theorem about larger tournaments.

value.rationale: The n=8 layer is the natural next complete cutoff after the established n<=7 torsion-free theorem and addresses an explicit foundational tournament torsion question. The result gives a new exact 26-profile integral homology distribution over all 6880 classes and raises the first possible torsion order to nine, including sharp beta1=6 and beta2=3 extrema. This exact complete natural finite invariant has mathematical value independent of a general infinite theorem or homotopy classification.

checked_sources: Resultary semantic searches (three query formulations; matching n<=7 and n=6 results)
final_claim: For every isomorphism class of tournaments T on exactly eight vertices (6880 classes), the directed out-neighborhood simplicial complex N+(T) has free reduced integral homology concentrated in degrees 0,1,2. Exactly 26 reduced Betti triples occur, with the complete multiplicities stated in RESULT.md and spectrum.csv. The largest beta0, beta1 and beta2 are respectively 1, 6 and 3; the unique beta1=6 tournament has the explicit representative given there. Combined with the independently published n<=7 result, any tournament with torsion in out-neighborhood integral homology requires at least nine vertices.
limitations: Finite exact census, no homotopy-type classification or n>=9 extrapolation.
